subject: radiology
title: Uterine artery embolisation in depth

steps.tx: Uterine artery embolisation blocks fibroid blood flow, so bulk, bleeding and pressure ease over months without a knife. The team counsels carefully when **fertility** matters, because ovarian reserve may dip and a future pregnancy needs planning. A **pedunculated subserosal fibroid** on a stalk risks detachment after embolisation, so surgical backup stays available for that patient. Pain peaks within hours after the procedure and the patient needs strong analgesia with anti inflammatory support. The flow in this step moves from mapping and counselling toward bilateral treatment and pain control in order.
steps.say: Uterine artery embolisation blocks fibroid blood flow so bulk and bleeding and pressure ease over months. The team counsels carefully when fertility matters because ovarian reserve may dip after treatment. A stalked outer fibroid risks detachment after embolisation so surgical backup stays available for safety. Pain peaks within hours after the procedure and the patient needs strong pain relief promptly. Careful mapping and counselling come first and bilateral treatment and pain control follow in order.

steps.tx: Complete uterine treatment needs both arteries, because collateral flow crosses the midline freely between the two sides. **Bilateral uterine embolisation** therefore closes both arteries in the same sitting whenever anatomy allows safe catheter positions. An **ovarian collateral** feeds the fibroid in some patients, and added closure completes treatment when that vessel dominates. The operator stops at a **pruning endpoint** short of complete stasis, which protects normal myometrium from unnecessary injury. A roadmap guides the microcatheter past cervicovaginal branches that the operator must spare during particle delivery.
steps.say: Complete uterine treatment needs both arteries because collateral flow crosses the midline freely between sides. A roadmap guides the microcatheter past vaginal branches that the operator must spare during delivery.

steps.tx: This pelvic angiogram is helpful because it shows both uterine arteries during fibroid embolisation, with a round fibroid blush in the centre. Contrast crosses the midline through a **midline crossover**, which proves why a single sided treatment would fail. The operator stops at a **pruning endpoint** on each side and spares the fine **ovarian collaterals** that appear at the edges. The image matters for the exam because bilateral closure with a restrained endpoint protects myometrium. That balance gives fibroid death without unnecessary injury to normal uterus.

steps.tx: A necrotic fibroid can leave the uterus through the cervix, and that event surprises patients after apparent success. **Fibroid expulsion** brings pain with discharge, and the patient may need hysteroscopic help to clear retained tissue. Dead tissue can also infect, so **infection after necrosis** declares with fever and needs antibiotics and sometimes removal of the uterus. Ovarian reserve that already runs low can fail after treatment and **early menopause** then follows in that patient. Most patients resume normal cycles, although the pattern varies during the first months after embolisation.

steps.tx: Follow up after uterine embolisation measures shrinkage and symptoms together rather than either outcome alone. **MRI at six months** quantifies fibroid death and the images combine with symptom scores for a full judgement. A patient who plans **pregnancy after treatment** waits for complete uterine healing and accepts specialist obstetric planning throughout. Regrowth with returning symptoms earns repeat embolisation or surgery after fresh imaging and counselling. **Satisfaction scores** track bleeding and bulk relief because patient reported relief defines success for this elective procedure.
